content: A woman who pursued legal action against the company faced severe harassment. A Chisso executive personally visited her, and her neighbors subjected her to intimidation. She was ignored, her family’s fishing boat was used without permission, their fishing nets were deliberately cut, and human feces were thrown at her in the street. The Litigation Group and their legal team received significant support from a grassroots national network of citizens' groups that emerged in 1969. These groups played a crucial role in raising awareness and funds for the lawsuit. The Kumamoto branch, in particular, was instrumental in advancing the case. In September 1969, they established a Trial Research Group, which included law professors, medical researchers (such as Masazumi Harada), sociologists, and even a housewife and poet, Michiko Ishimure. This group provided valuable materials to strengthen the lawyers’ legal arguments. Their report, titled Corporate Responsibility for Minamata Disease: Chisso's Illegal Acts, published in August 1970, became the foundation for the lawsuit's eventual success. The trial lasted nearly four years, during which the Litigation Group’s lawyers sought to prove Chisso’s corporate negligence. They had to address three critical legal points to win the case. First, they needed to demonstrate that methylmercury caused Minamata disease and that the company’s factory was the source of the pollution. This was relatively straightforward due to extensive research conducted by Kumamoto University and government findings. Second, they had to establish that the company could and should have foreseen the harmful effects of its wastewater and taken preventive measures, thus proving negligence in their duty of care. Third, they had to challenge the validity of the 1959 sympathy money agreement, which prohibited patients from seeking further compensation. The trial included testimonies from patients and their families, but the most impactful evidence came from Chisso executives and employees. A particularly dramatic testimony was given by Hajime Hosokawa on July 4, 1970, from his hospital bed, where he was dying of cancer. He described his experiments with cats, including the infamous Cat 400, which developed Minamata disease after being fed factory wastewater. He also revealed his opposition to the 1958 decision to redirect wastewater from Hyakken Harbour to the Minamata River. His testimony was corroborated by a colleague, who disclosed that company officials had ordered them to stop their cat experiments in the autumn of 1959. Tragically, Hosokawa passed away three months after his testimony. Former factory manager Eiichi Nishida admitted that the company prioritized profits over safety, leading to hazardous working conditions and negligence in handling mercury. Former Chisso President Kiichi Yoshioka confessed that the company promoted a false theory blaming dumped World War II explosives for the pollution, despite knowing it was baseless. On March 20, 1973, the court delivered a verdict that was a complete victory for the patients of the Litigation Group. The court invalidated the 1959 sympathy money agreement and ordered Chisso to make one-time payments of JPY 18 million (USD 66,000) for each deceased patient and between JPY 16 million and JPY 18 million (USD 59,000 to USD 66,000) for each surviving patient. This was the largest sum ever awarded by a Japanese court at the time. While the arbitration and litigation groups continued their struggles against Chisso, a new group of Minamata disease sufferers emerged. To qualify for compensation under the 1959 agreement, patients had to be officially recognized by ad hoc certification committees based on their symptoms. However, these committees adhered to a rigid interpretation of Minamata disease, requiring patients to exhibit all symptoms of Hunter-Russell Syndrome, the standard diagnosis for organic mercury poisoning at the time, which originated from a 1940 industrial accident in the United Kingdom. This strict criterion led to many applicants being rejected, leaving them confused and frustrated. A key figure in the fight for uncertified patients was Teruo Kawamoto, born in 1931 as the seventh son of a Chisso worker and local fisherman. From 1959 onwards, his father began showing typical symptoms of Minamata disease, including numbness in his hands and feet, slurred speech, impaired walking, and restricted vision. His condition deteriorated until he was admitted to a mental hospital where Teruo worked. Suffering from hallucinations and suicidal tendencies, his father eventually lost the ability to recognize anyone and died in April 1965, with Teruo by his side. As of March 2001, 2,265 victims had been officially certified (1,784 of whom had died), and over 10,000 people had received financial compensation from Chisso, although they were not recognized as official victims. Quantifying the full impact of Minamata disease remains challenging, as no comprehensive epidemiological study has been conducted, and patients were only recognized if they voluntarily applied to a Certification Council for financial compensation. Many victims faced discrimination and ostracism from their communities if they disclosed their symptoms. Some feared the disease was contagious, and many locals remained loyal to Chisso, as their livelihoods depended on the company. This environment discouraged sufferers from seeking certification. Despite these challenges, over 17,000 people applied for certification. The Certification Council’s decisions were heavily influenced by economic and political factors surrounding Minamata and the Chisso corporation, rather than being purely based on medical recognition. Compensation for victims also caused ongoing strife within the community, including unfounded accusations that some claimants were not genuine sufferers of the disease. According to Timothy S. George, the environmental protests surrounding Minamata disease contributed to the democratization of Japan. Initially, the rights of the victims were not acknowledged, and they received no compensation. Instead, they were ostracized due to ignorance about the disease, as people feared it was contagious. Those directly affected by the pollution of Minamata Bay were initially excluded from participating in decisions that would shape their future.
